TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 9 NOVEMBER 2022 AT 10 AM (AEST)
DAY 10
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR A VIAL, for the Commonwealth
MR BRADY, on instructions from Clayton Utz, for Ms Wilson

COMMISSIONER: Yes, what appearances today?
MR GREGGERY: Commissioner, I appear with Ms Marsh today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear today with Mr Vial.
COMMISSIONER: And?
MR BRADY: [Inaudible] Instructed by Clayton Utz on behalf of the first witness, Ms Wilson.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks Mr Brady. Ms Wilson, will you take an oath or an affirmation? An
affirmation.
<SERENA JUDITH WILSON, AFFIRMED.
<EXAMINATION BY MR GREGGERY KC
COMMISSIONER: Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner. Can you tell the Commission your full name,
please?
MS WILSON: Serena Judith Wilson.
MR GREGGERY: You were formerly the Deputy Secretary of the Department of Social
Services?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Ms Wilson, you received or rather a notice to give a statement and produce
documents dated 28 October 2022, identified NTG-0066. That's correct?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you produced a statement on 31 October 2022 in response?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And then again yesterday, you produced a further statement in response to
that notice. Both of those statements referred to various documents?
MS WILSON: Yes.

COMMISSIONER: Alright. The documents in the schedule will be numbered in accordance
with the numbers in the schedule, 1208 to 1219.
<EXHIBITS 1208 TO 1219 AS PER THE SCHEDULE
MR GREGGERY: Thank you, Commissioner.
I might just start with a very broad overview, and if we go back to the evidence last week, if
Exhibit 61, DSS.5002.0001.0001, could be placed on the screen. Ms Wilson, this is just an
organisational chart from November 2015. And if the boxes on the left side of that under
Ms Wilson's name could be called out. Thank you. Sorry, I think I said November '15, but I
meant November 2014. Ms Wilson, that's, in terms of the organisational structure, where
you sat as Deputy Secretary in late 2014?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And of relevance to the evidence that you will give today are various people
whose names appear in that organisational chart. There's a Cath Halbert. You can see that?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Andrew Whitecross, on the box on the right-hand side on the second row?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: His name appears in the second box on the second row as well? And I think
there's a reference there to Ian Joyce acting in that position at that point in time?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And further down the list, you can see a Murray Kimber in the middle box
on the bottom row? And did you have a close working relationship with each of those
persons?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: How would you describe their positions? Yours is the Deputy Secretary level
position. What are theirs?
MS WILSON: So if I start at the next level under me.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: Cath Halbert was a senior executive service band two. We called them Group
Managers. Andrew Whitecross was acting as a Group Manager doing work, as that box

next level with a Mr Ian Joyce acting for him. And then down below - so that's a senior
executive service band one position, or a branch head, Assistant Secretary. And at the
bottom in the middle box, Mr Murray Kimber was also an Assistant Secretary, senior
executive service band one.
MR GREGGERY: And you were on the senior executive service band as well, I understand?
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And what level were you?
MS WILSON: A senior executive service band three, which was a Deputy Secretary.
MR GREGGERY: Your role, or the Division is described as Social Security. What did that
entail?
MS WILSON: So it was broad social security policy, broader strategic policy. And there was a
lot of work being done on welfare reform arising out of a report that had been presented to
government by Mr Patrick McClure. I can't recall the exact date, I'm sorry, but sometime in
2014.
MR GREGGERY: And do you recall that that report, the McClure report, was released
publicly in 2015?
MS WILSON: I believe it may - it was in 2014.
MR GREGGERY: I will come back to that. The responsibilities, of course, as you've described
them broadly, encompass what are described in the various branches below you as well.
And can you describe, then, the relationship between your position in the Department of
Social Services and any corresponding position in the Department of Human Services?
MS WILSON: Yes. So our responsibilities were essentially the high-level policy that related
to - flowing from the legislation of the Social Security Act. Issues that governments may
want to explore from time to time that went to how social security payments worked and
might change. Also broader social policy interactions. So, for example, how social security
policy and payments might interact with elements of the tax system, with elements of
eligibility for other community and human services.
And I guess issues around emerging pressures for low-income people in a sort of strategic
and social policy sense, including the evidence for what sorts of interventions would make a
difference to reduce the likelihood of people requiring social security support in the first
instance, or assist them to leave the social security system and become self-reliant and
move into the workforce. And we did a lot of that work with colleagues in the Department
of Employment.
In the Department of Human Services, my counterparts were more responsible for the

experience, how individuals were experiencing the system, what decision-making was
occurring, the responsiveness of the delivery system through its various channels, including
call centres, office-based interactions, online interactions in terms of how people in
Australia experience the social security system. That's probably not comprehensive, I'm
sorry.
MR GREGGERY: I understand. And I wasn't asking for the most comprehensive answer, just a
broad outline. You've described aspects of legislative and policy responsibility on the part of
DSS. In the day-to-day work of DSS how are those matters related to the service delivery
aspects undertaken by DHS?
MS WILSON: So I guess the architecture that supports the relationship is really underpinned
very much by the Guide to the Social Security Law. So the Guide is a set of online resources
that the Department of Social Services and in its many forms previously maintained to assist
decision-makers in the Department of Human Services, and as the overarching authority, I
guess, of translating both the Social Security Act and the Social Security (Administration) Act
into a somewhat more accessible form, I guess and a more, perhaps, intuitive form but with
authority from the Act that could then have procedural guidelines or ICT systems that were
being developed in the Department of Human Services, follow.
So it was in a sense the bible or the authoritative document - and it wasn't a document it
was an online resource. It was also often used by the public or other interested parties,
including advocacy organisations and the like, as a resource by them as well.
MR GREGGERY: That is, it provided a level of authoritative guidance about the application of
existing social security law from DSS, who was responsible for those areas of legislation?
MS WILSON: That's correct. And it's also relevant in the sense that the Social Services
Secretary had a express delegation through the position in the legislation that was known as
the Chief Executive for the Commonwealth Services Delivery Agency, which previously had
been Centrelink but became part of the Department of Human Services. And it was under
that express delegation with a series of other delegations for which, as I recall, the
Australian Government Solicitor prepared an instrument, it was under that set of
delegations that individual officers in the Department of Human Services would make
decisions and the service delivery system would reflect the law.
MR GREGGERY: I may have missed what you said at the start of your answer about the
source of the delegation. Did the original authority, covered by the delegation, rest with the
Secretary of the Department of Social Services?
MS WILSON: Yes, and I believe - I haven't had the opportunity to refresh my memory in any
detail since receiving the notice, but I believe the expressed delegation is reflected in the
Social Security (Administration) Act.
MR GREGGERY: Right. Just give me a moment. And so the responsibility for implementing
the social security law and administering it was delegated under that series of delegations

MS WILSON: It wasn't actually, as I recall, the Secretary of the Department of Human
Services. I believe it was actually one of the Secretaries' deputies who was identified within
their structure as the Chief Executive of the Commonwealth Services Delivery Agency. And
this is a little historical, but it relates to before Human Services was formed and Centrelink
was the agency which then subsequently became absorbed into Human Services.
MR GREGGERY: I see. To your knowledge, the position of Chief Executive of the Department
of Human Services continued in that role. That is, the delegated role?
MS WILSON: Yes. As I understand it, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Who in the area supervised by you or overseen by you, stayed on top of the
Guide to Social Security Law?
MS WILSON: Every area had a responsibility within their own policy remit. So, for
example - where can I look - in terms of Rates and Means Testing Policy, the position that
was the Assistant Secretary occupied by Ian Joyce on this chart, others over time, and
substantively by Andrew Whitecross would have been the area that maintained and
identified the need for changes to the Guide in respect of rates and means testing. So how
the rate calculators worked, how the means test worked.
The position occupied by - another example would be Ms Michalina Stawyskyj on the
left-hand side for Age, Disability and Carer payments, that position would have looked at
and been responsible for the essential eligibility criteria for an aged pension or a Disability
Support Pension, or a carer payment, but not the specific rate or the specific means test. So
it would have been the, if you like, the entry eligibility that went to age of the person, their
residency or citizenship status and those characteristics.
Whereas their means, their level of assets, their level of income both earned and, for many
pensioners, unearned income and how they were to be assessed and how they related to
eligibility would have been taken care of by the Assistant Secretary of Rates and Means
Testing Policy as part of the Guide. So that it was a, if you like subject matter-specific
responsibility, and it was generally at that Assistant Secretary level, as I recall.
MR GREGGERY: Much of what you've described would be reflected in the various Acts, the
social security law?
MS WILSON: Yes, that's correct. So social security law would have been the overarching
architecture and the legal authority, and the Guide was a translation of that with - and as I
recall, it had hyperlinks to the section of - so electronically it had an active link to the section
of the Act. But it might provide a bit more interpretational guidance - well, it certainly was
intended to provide more guidance for decision-makers in the Department of Human
Services and for, importantly, the construction of - of the way - the way that the various ICT
systems or delivery arrangements implemented decision-making on the ground.

MR GREGGERY: And is it your understanding, or your experience, or both, that DHS would
implement or establish their own delivery protocols - for want of a better term - underneath
the Guide to Social Security?
MS WILSON: So it was my understanding - and I didn't work in the Department of Human
Services - that they might develop procedural guidelines, for example.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS WILSON: To help their staff that would supplement the Guide as a resource for them.
MR GREGGERY: But clearly any implementation or process questions determined by DHS
from your position had to accord with the Guide to Social Security Law developed under
your remit?
MS WILSON: That was our expectation, yes, and I believe - well, it was a long-standing
practice.
MR GREGGERY: And that was so for two reasons, I take it. One was the Guide to Social
Security Law reflected social security legislative requirements, but also the relationship
between the two Departments was that DSS was responsible, as you have indicated, for
legislative and policy areas and DHS broadly responsible for implementation and process
and delivery aspects.
MS WILSON: And the day-to-day decision-making in particular, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. I will come back to your counterparts in DHS, but can we deal firstly
with questions of legal advice - this is on a broad process level within DSS that might affect
social security law. Obviously, you were at the Deputy Secretary level. The Department had
legal advisers internally. How was the line of reporting between that area, the legal area
within DSS and your office, undertaken on a day-to-day basis?
MS WILSON: Generally, the need for a change to legislation - I guess it could arise in several
ways. Often, it was part of a budget process where there was a new policy proposal that
would identify that something had legal implications and, therefore, required legislative
change, and the relevant group manager, the level below me, and Assistant Secretary
through their staff - and depending on the nature of the change, how significant it was,
would - and usually, as I recall, it might be someone at the - what was called the Director
level.
So a non-senior executive service person with subject matter expertise might be the key
liaison point with our Legal Services colleagues to secure that advice. Then it was usually
discussed, and it depends how many parties there were to it, in general terms. Was it
confined to one area of responsibility with the Department or was it across a number of
payments and a number of areas? And depending on its importance, it could be escalated
further up the chain.

Really to me on a day-to-day basis, as I recall, and often put together with issues that were
not necessarily legal but were policy of nature. So is this consistent? Does it cohere with our
broader approach to policy in these areas? Does it encompass, perhaps, some of the related
reform agendas that government has asked us to look at? How does it interact with other
elements of important issues? So there was usually work to bring both - together both those
specific legal advices as it related to the Act and its provisions.
And at times it was simply the Social Security Act, at other times it may be the Social Security
(Administration) Act, depending on the subject matter. But that was put together with some
policy discussion and analysis to bring together a view about - particularly if it were a new
idea - its merits, the issues that might be identified and the risks and the extent of change
that might be required, and any commentary on coherence, other interactions, relevance,
sensitivity and the like.
MR GREGGERY: And so, on a day-to-day basis, that was undertaken primarily at an executive
level officer?
MS WILSON: It was usually undertaken - I beg your pardon.
MR GREGGERY: Yes, that’s it.
MR WILSON: It was usually undertaken by - it depended on the depth of expertise and the
complexity of the issue. It was certainly under the oversight or by someone at the Director
level. Sometimes it if it was a small, confined issue, the individual who was requested to
seek the advice after a discussion with the Director might be at a level below that. But the
Director would, I believe, invariably be involved.
But it would be visible to and understood by the Assistant Secretary that that advice was
being sought, and depending on how important it was, usually escalated to a senior
executive service band two and sometimes a senior executive service band three,
depending on the issue.
MR GREGGERY: That is, the more significant the legal question or policy question, or the
relationship between legal and policy, the higher it reached in terms of the part of the
Department overseen by you?
MS WILSON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: And on occasion it would reach you, if it was of particular significance?
MS WILSON: That's correct.
MR GREGGERY: What about your - the division of responsibility between yourself as Deputy
Secretary in this area, and the Secretary, Mr Pratt?
MS WILSON: So I'm not quite sure I understand your question.

MR GREGGERY: You have described all of the aspects that you're responsible for. Is there
any professional areas, policy areas, legal areas - any of those teams that you are required
to report to Mr Pratt about or that he expected you to report to him about?
MS WILSON: Certainly, on key significant DSS initiatives, we would have regular contact.
Very significant changes in the budget, for example, we would discuss them, perhaps ahead
of meetings with Ministers. We would certainly discuss them in preparing the portfolio
budget submission documentation and various budget documents. We would discuss - and
often he would see material in writing ahead of those meetings and we would do briefings
for him. We would work through with him to aid his understanding of the issues.
So, for example, in the 2015-16 Budget, there were a range of quite significant changes to
the social security going through, one of which were a set of changes to the way the assets
tests for pensions and other payments worked. And Mr Pratt, because he was expected
to - or he did as regularly, as the Secretary of the Department, go into the Expenditure
Review Committee with the Minister for Social Services, he would need to be quite well
versed in at times a level of detail about those changes.
So we would iteratively prepare material for him. And it was not infrequent that Mr Pratt,
myself, a senior executive service band two and possibly an Assistant Secretary or some
other subject matter expert would have discussions on DSS proposals with the Minister,
with advisors present. So, for example, that did happen on those assets test changes - assets
tests taper changes.
MR GREGGERY: And your means of communication with Mr Pratt in his role as Secretary
and your role as Deputy Secretary, did it take a number of forms?
MS WILSON: Yes. So we had a regular catch-up meeting, which I believe was once a
fortnight. It's a long time ago, I'm sorry, but my recollection is it was generally once a
fortnight. And so we identify issues that we both wanted to discuss - not in any formal way.
We usually have our little list that we would take in. I would have a notebook with things to
discuss and actions to be taken. So actions that I intended to undertake, and then I would
tick off actions to be taken and perhaps a note about next step or something like that. It
wasn't an official record.
Often there would be phone calls between us. Often there would be emails on the fly. On
occasion - and not infrequently, but when there were significant issues that were DSS new
policy approaches - for example, the assets test taper that I'm talking about - we would
workshop material ahead of a meeting with the Minister. Maybe some graphics that we
wished to present to the Minister, some data. Those sorts of things. So there would be a
pack that we would put together with copies of briefs that had gone up on the issue and
other resources so that he was well-versed and knew what the Minister had received.
And I believe he - I can't recall, but I believe he would have seen copies of quite significant
briefs. And certainly we would - the budget area of the Department ahead of Expenditure
Review Committee meetings and the like - and he would have a meeting with the Minister

would do a workshop with key people, myself and others, perhaps, in areas of my
responsibility, colleagues and their - subject matter experts in their areas of responsibility to
make sure that he was well equipped on the Department of Social Services' new policy
proposals.
Issues that arose in the Green Brief that the Department of Finance put together where they
were making commentary, and that was often used as a guide for those meetings on
proposals so there was nothing that blindsided him. So it was very fast-paced, quick moving,
a lot of material. So there were a number of different ways that we would try to keep
Mr Pratt across issues.
MR GREGGERY: The regular catch-up which may have occurred on a fortnightly basis, would
your executive assistants or personal assistants attend those meetings?
MS WILSON: No. It was one-on-one.
MR GREGGERY: It was one-on-one. And were they diary entries or calendar entries on a
regular basis?
MS WILSON: I believe they were calendar entries on a regular basis, but sometimes there
were lots of competing appointments, so often it would slip and then you would get notice
that - that he can do it tomorrow morning, and I can't recall whether there would be a
calendar entry or something else would run over. But there would be an opportunity for 30
minutes or the like. Mr Pratt was at the time also advancing significant issues around aged
care and childcare, because they had come into the portfolio when it was established in
2013. And there was a very significant reform agenda in a number of areas outside my own
responsibilities.
MR GREGGERY: You indicated in an answer to a statement a little while - a question a little
while ago that it's been some time.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you also referred to making diary entries or notebook entries of things
to discuss and actions item taken. And you retired effective August 2018.
MS WILSON: In reality, it was June 2018. So I had some leave that I took ahead of my official
retirement, which was on 31 August 2018. However, I left the building - I believe it was
actually - I believe my last day in harness, one might say, was the Friday of the first week of
June. I beg your pardon, I haven't had the opportunity to check what date that actually was.
But I believe my last activity for the Department was appearing in the Senate Estimates in
that 2018-19 Budget, so after that day, I had no contact with - no access to. I handed my ICT
back. I left it behind.
And prior to that, I did a big clean-up of my office and the like. So my memory is I took the
technology in. Possibly, it was the - I can't recall whether Estimates was the Thursday or the

computer and all the other bits and pieces in on the Friday. But I had been doing a clean-up
of the office ahead of then.
MR GREGGERY: In one of your statements - I think it's your first one - you indicate that
following your retirement or leaving the office, you destroyed all of the notebooks that
recorded the lists that were developed in the regular catch-up with Mr Pratt?
MS WILSON: I can't recall exactly when that was. It would have been part of cleaning out my
office for the new occupant. And they weren't - as I indicated in my statement, they were
not official records. They were personal jottings that were mainly lists. And so it was
standard practice, I believe, to do that. I had no intention of having any ongoing Australian
public service employment. Somebody else was going to be doing my job from that point
on. So, yes, they were destroyed.
MR GREGGERY: Ms Wilson, you have referred to the regular face-to-face catch-ups when
only yourself and Mr Pratt were present. Telephone calls, emails, the development of
iterative briefings for matters of significance. What about forms of messaging or instant
messaging?
MS WILSON: No. Well, we would have done possibly text messaging, but I - I'm - I didn't
come to things like WhatsApp until very recently.
MR GREGGERY: The documents that you have had access to, then, in preparing your
statement fall into two categories. There are broad departmental documents, you might
say, and then there are emails sent and received by you. In respect of those emails,
they - you describe a secure and non-secure email account. Can you explain that?
MS WILSON: So there were two systems that operated at the time. One was an Outlook
product, and they were emails that had general day-to-day transactional information on
them, but you wouldn't use them to attach a secure document, for example. The secure
enclave, as we called it, was used for the transmission of documents that were of the
protected status that might end up becoming documents for cabinet. So draft material and
final material for the Expenditure Review Committee. Discussions in preparation, the
development of new policy ideas that - and the like.
We used to see things like decisions from - and correspondence that related to cabinet
issues and the like in that system. I haven’t had – I had the opportunity on Friday to review
some of my emails, and I believe there were more than - and the process of that required
me to go physically into Canberra - I live outside Canberra - and look at on a tablet an
archived version of the emails, both the Outlook and the Enclave from the period. I believe
it was 2014 through to my departure. There were more than 8,000 emails not easily
searchable. I did try to identify some that were relevant to my statement at that time.
MR GREGGERY: Was it your understanding or a result of a request by you, that the
8,000-odd emails were produced for your inspection?

MS WILSON: In that form that I describe. So I only had access to them on Friday morning last
week. Maybe about 10.30, I was able to physically go into the premises of the
Attorney-General's Department. It took some time, and I needed some assistance to make
sure that I could understand how to use the tablet and the records. It was not an easy
searchable process. And then to ask for anything to be printed, as I could not take that
physically away with me, they had to be individually saved to the tablet I was using and then
put on to a USB to then be taken away physically to be printed, so that I might take them
home with me to help prepare my supplementary statement.
And there were a number that were produced for me. There were a number that I did not
receive on Friday that I didn't - I didn't inspect the bundle that I took away with me at that
point. I had some - other appointments on the course of Friday. When I looked at them on
Saturday morning, I noticed that there were a couple of things attached to emails that I
requested be printed and they hadn't been. And some of those documents I believe I still
have not seen, they were cabinet-in-confidence documents. However, I did have a number
of resources available to me. A small number that I relied upon to produce my
supplementary statement.
MR GREGGERY: When you say "resources" do you mean emails that - - -
MS WILSON: I mean the documents that I took away with me and some other documents, a
small number, that had been provided to me in the period between the lodgement of my
first statement on Monday, the 31st. So I received some soft copies and accessed some hard
copies of documents. So some were sent to me through the Attorney-General's Department
Royal Commission Coordination Area, and they had come from DSS, and they had been
identified as documents that were relevant from my appearance as a witness and my
statements.
Beg your pardon, there was also an index - an Excel spreadsheet index with over 1000
entries that I received on - it may have been Friday, 28th or Saturday, 29th October with
numbers down the left-hand side identifying whether the document was a DSS or a
Commonwealth document, and a date and a high-level description of what the document
might include. That was a non-searchable, if you like, not smart product. And so I did look
through that Excel spreadsheet over the course of preparing my initial statement to identify
what might be relevant to support that.
And I was able to physically go in and look at those documents on the morning of Monday,
31st October. And, again, there were hyperlinks to the documents on the tablet that I was
able to use at the AGS premises in Canberra. And I could ask for a number of those to be
printed, which I did, which added some information in respect of my first statement. And
then I subsequently, I believe, requested some additional documents from that index and
had other documents from that index sent to me in the course of - I believe it was Tuesday,
the 1st, the evening of Monday, the 31st to help me prepare - for me to consider.
And it was on Wednesday, the - 2nd or perhaps the evening of Tuesday, the 1st. I'm sorry, I
can't quite recall. It's been a fairly frenetic few days - week or so. I recognise the need to

the Thursday, 3rd of November, it would have been, to again use the tablet - I still didn't
have my emails at that point - and go through the index of the Excel spreadsheet with the
links and ask for some more printing to be done to help support my supplementary
statement.
MR GREGGERY: Your initial statement and your supplementary statement do not annexe a
large number of documents it. It might be less than 15 in total between them. One of the
questions you were asked in the notice was to identify your knowledge of any
communication of the 2014 advice to Finn Pratt. You haven't been able to identify a
document which records that communication in the thousands that you have been
provided?
MS WILSON: No, I haven't. I have been able to identify the intention, that I expressed to
speak with Mr Pratt in respect of the - an approach from the Department of Human Services
in February 2015. I beg your pardon.
MR GREGGERY: We will come to the document in due course. But my question was limited
to the fact there was no documentary communication of the 2014 advice in your searches.
MS WILSON: No. No.
MR GREGGERY: Does that indicate to you that the searches are incomplete, given what
you've said about the extent of communication on significant issues?
MS WILSON: Yes, that - I don't know. I don't know whether there would be evidence that
there was a direct communication. The environment was very fast moving. There were
often discussions about ideas to be developed, and depending on their significance and how
well advanced they were, it would vary as to whether or not there was a record that goes to
the outcome of a discussion and the like.
MR GREGGERY: But not even the outcome, the anticipation of.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And you have located neither.
MS WILSON: No, I haven't. And generally, as I identify, if something was a DSS proposal,
there would be much more documentary evidence. Proposals that came from other places,
perhaps not, because we were working in conjunction with that Department, and it
depended on whether it came forward at any point. Moreover, we tended to rely on more
face-to-face discussion, and I would use my personal notebook, I guess, as the way of
making sure that I had raised something and ticking off that I - that I had.
MR GREGGERY: Surely a more accurate way, as part of your official responsibilities and
Mr Pratt's responsibilities to record that you had communicated information of significance
to him would not be in the personal notebook but would be in the form of a memo or an

MS WILSON: Yes. For DSS proposals that were progressing through the budget process, that
would generally be not a memo, but an email. I have not been able to identify anything from
that period in relation to the questions that I was asked that takes that form. It is evident
from my statements that I intended to discuss the issue with Mr Pratt. I cannot
independently recall whether I did at that point in time.
MR GREGGERY: You are aware that the DHS proposal became a budget proposal.
MS WILSON: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: That is, a new policy proposal and then made its way from that point
forward into the budget, as you have said. Was that done under the banner of DSS or DHS?
MS WILSON: It was a DHS proposal.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. But insofar as responsibility for that goes, that's a DSS responsibility,
isn't it?
MS WILSON: If one looks at Budget Paper Number 2, which is the budget measures paper,
that is, the documentation that's released publicly for all measures in a budget or a mid-year
and economic forecast, there is assigned a responsibility of a portfolio to the measure. At
that time in the 2015-16 Budget, the Strengthening the Integrity of the Welfare Payments is
listed under the Department of Human Services in terms of the investment associated with
implementation of that measure.
